The opening with the Prophet ﷺ being commanded to glorify the name of his Lord by speech (*tasbih*, glorification, meaning declaring God free of all imperfections) indicates that after this he will be given glad tidings and good news. That is His saying: ﴿He will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6], and the verses that follow, as will come. In this there is the skill of an opening (*bara'at al-istihlal*, the art of a strong opening).

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ.

*Tasbih* is declaring God free of deficiencies. It is one of the words that may not be attached to anything other than the name of God Most High. Likewise, the verbs derived from it do not take a direct object in the accusative (as a patient) except for what is a name of God. The same applies to the verbal nouns derived from it, such as *Subhan Allah* (Glory be to God). It is among the religious concepts, so it seems likely that it was transferred into Arabic from Hebrew. This was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Since the command to glorify is here connected to a name, it is clear that what is commanded is a speech that indicates God's transcendence, by way of stating good reports, or by describing Him with sacred attributes, to establish them for what points to His essence, Most High, from names and meanings. Since these are speeches, they relate to the name of God by virtue of its indication of the Essence. So what is commanded is the stating of noble reports and exalted attributes about the names that indicate God Most High, such as proper names, attributes, and the like. This returns to declaring the Named One free of imperfection through those names.

For this reason, the Qur'an frequently ties glorification to the word "name of God," as in His saying: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74]. This was discussed earlier in the discussion of the basmala at the beginning of this commentary.

So glorifying the name of God is the utterance of His transcendence in private and among people, with a mention befitting His majesty, through beliefs and deeds, such as prostration and praise. This includes the speaker's bringing to mind the meanings of the words of glorification, since the purpose of speech is its meaning. And by the combination of uttering and bringing the meaning to mind, the meaning is repeated in the speaker's mind and what is in his soul of the magnification of God Most High is renewed.

As for the servant's reflection on God's greatness and his repeating of His transcendence in his mind, this is glorification of God's essence and of what His name denotes, but it is not called glorification of the name of God, because that does not apply to a word of God's names. So this is glorification of God's essence, not glorification of His name.

This is the criterion for distinguishing between the word *tasbih* connected to the word "name of God," as in ﴿glorify the name of your Lord﴾, and its connection without a name, as in ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him and glorify Him﴾ [al-Insan: 26], and ﴿and they glorify Him and to Him they prostrate﴾ [al-A'raf: 206]. This is the basis of the distinction between the use of ﴿glorify the name of your Lord﴾ and the use of "and glorify Him." Both expressions ultimately have one meaning, because both are intended as guidance to knowing that God is free of imperfections.

For what is obligated to be timed is speech and action, not beliefs. Another example is the verb governing a preposition *bi* (with), as in His saying: ﴿and they glorified with the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah: 15], since praise is speech, so it accompanies only a similar speech.

Defining a name by way of attribution to "your Lord," rather than defining it by attribution to the name of Majesty (Allah), as in "glorify the name of God," is because of what the word "Lord" (*rabb*) implies, namely that He is the Creator who manages. As for attributing "Lord" to the pronoun of the Messenger ﷺ, it is to honor him with this attribution and so that he has a share beyond the obligation to glorify.

Then the word "your Lord" is followed by the description "the Most High" and what comes after it of relative clauses that indicate the operations of His power. So He deserves glorification for the attributes of His essence and for the attributes of His bestowal of favor upon people by creating them in the best form, guiding them, and providing for them and for their livestock. This is an allusion to the requirement of the command to glorify His name: that He is worthy of transcendence, because of His essence and because He is described as the Creator of creatures, a creation that indicates knowledge, wisdom, and perfection of craftsmanship, and because He has bestowed guidance and provision, by which the human condition is set right in soul and body. The first three attributes were chosen for their suitability to the aim of the surah, as we will explain.

The word *al-a'la* (the Most High) is a noun that indicates an increase in the attribute of height, that is, elevation. Elevation is counted, in people's custom, as a perfection. So height is not attributed without restriction except to something that is not blameworthy by custom. For this reason, when no object of comparison is mentioned with the attribute of "the Most High," it indicates absolute superiority, as in His description here. For this reason, it is related that Pharaoh said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24].

The elevation from which His description as "the Most High" is derived is a metaphorical elevation, which is complete and perpetual perfection.

Al-Ghazali said: "Elevation in the rational rank is like elevation in sensory gradations, and an example of a rational degree is the difference between cause and effect, principle and derivative, agent and recipient, perfect and deficient." End of quote.

The choice of this description in this surah is because it contains exaltation of the Qur'an, and firmness in receiving it, and what it contains of reminder. This is due to the high status of the Qur'an, so it belongs to what relates to the attribute of divine elevation, since it is His speech.

This attribute is the foundation of the rule for interpreting God's attributes and carrying them to what befits the description "the Most High." For this reason it is obligatory to interpret the ambiguous (*mutashabihat*) attributes.

It has been said that from His saying ﴿glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ comes the supplication of prostration in prayer, since it is reported that the one prostrating should say: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," so that he joins the effect of glorification by action with the effect of glorification by speech.

The clause ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ contains two attributes: the attribute of creation, and the attribute of proportioning what was created. The object of "created" is omitted. It may be understood as general, which is what the majority of exegetes assumed, and what is related from 'Ata'. This is the normal treatment of an omitted object when no indicator points to it. That is, He created every created thing. This is like His saying, quoting Moses: ﴿Our Lord is the One who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50].

It may also be understood as specific: that is, He created man, as Zajjaj assumed, or He created Adam, as is related from al-Dahhak. This is indicated by the linking of the verb "created" with the verb "proportioned." He said: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29], and the verse continues.

He joined the clause "and proportioned" with the particle *fa* (then/so) rather than *wa* (and), to indicate that its content is the aim of the relative clause, and that what precedes it is a preparation for it, as in the verse of Ibn Zayyaba:

*Alas for Zayyaba, for al-Harith the dawn-raider,*
*then the spoiler, then the one who returns.*

Because grief is justified when he attacks them at dawn, takes their wealth, and returns with it, and they cannot defend against him or recover it.

So the *fa* in His saying "fa-sawwa" (and so proportioned) is for sequence in mention, on the reckoning that creation is prior in the mind to proportioning, even though the achievement of proportioning occurs together with the achievement of creation.

*Taswiya* (proportioning) is the making equal of what He created. If it is taken in its general sense, proportioning means making every kind and type of existing thing suited, that is, appropriate to the actions that are in its nature. The bending of the scorpion's tail is from the proportioning of its creation, so that it may repel by means of it, with ease, what would harm it.

Because proportioning is simultaneous with creation, he connected it to the verb "created" with the particle *fa*, which indicates causation: that is, proportioning is the result that follows from creation.

*Taqdir* (determining) means the placing of measure and bringing it into being in things, in their essences and powers. It is said *qaddara* with the doubled letter and *qadara* without it, with the same meaning.

The majority read *qaddara* with the doubled letter, and al-Kisa'i alone read it without doubling.

*Miqdar* (measure) originally means the quantity of a thing that is measured by a cubit, a measure, a weight, or counting. Here it is applied to the formation of creatures in orderly, consistent manners, through the composition of visible bodily parts, such as the two hands, and inner parts, such as the heart, and through the placement of intellectual powers, such as sense perception, capacity, and the skills of craft.

The repetition of the relative pronoun in His saying "and He who determined" and His saying "and He who brought forth the pasture," together with the conjunction letter being sufficient without repetition, is for the emphasis on each relative clause and the affirmation of each of them of what the relative pronoun refers to. This is among the requirements of elaboration (*itnab*, amplification).

The conjunction of His saying "fa-hada" (and so guided) is like the conjunction of "fa-sawwa." If "created" and "determined" are taken as general in their object, the guidance is general.

What was said about the reason for joining "fa-hada" with *fa* is like what was said about joining "fa-sawwa."

The joining of "fa-hada" to "qaddara" is the joining of the effect to the cause. That is, He guided every determined thing

[Page 277]

to what was determined for it. The guidance of man and of the kinds of animals that have perception and will is the guidance of inspiration to the manner of using what was determined in them, of measures and powers, in what suits their use. So whenever a thing comes into existence through the effects of that determining, guidance to carrying it out is achieved through its effect.

The meaning is: He determined all things and guided them to the performance of their functions as they were determined. So when God determined for man that he should be able to speak, to know, and to craft, through the reason and bodily instruments He gave him, He guided him to use his thought for what attains what he was created for. And when He determined that the cow should give milk, He inspired it to graze and to call to its calf, so that it would thereby give milk to the milker. And when He determined the bee for producing honey, He inspired it to feed on flowers and fruits, and inspired it to build the hive and its hexagonal cells in which it places the honey.

If the object of "created" is taken as specific, namely man, then the object of "determined" is parallel to it: that is, the determining of the full powers of man. And the guidance would be a specific guidance, namely the indication of perception and reason.

The two descriptions of proportioning and guidance were chosen among the attributes of actions that are favors upon people and that indicate God Most High's deserving of transcendence, because these two attributes have a suitability to what the surah contains. For He who proportions the Prophet's ﷺ creation in a way that suits what he was created for, namely bearing the burdens of prophethood, will not fail to prepare him to preserve what is revealed to him, to make it easy for him, and to give him a law suited to that ease. He said: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6], and He said: ﴿and We will ease you toward ease﴾ [al-A'la: 8].

His words, ﴿And He who brought forth the pasture﴾, are a reminder of the creation of the whole category of plants, including trees and others. He limited the reference to one of its kinds, which is *al-kala'* (herbage), because it is the sustenance of the grazing animals (*al-sawa'im*) from which people benefit.

[Page 278 continues]

The intended meaning is His bringing it out of the earth, which is His causing it to grow.

*Al-mar'a* (the pasture) is the vegetation that grazing animals feed upon. Its origin is either a *masdar mimi* (a verbal noun formed with the prefix *mim*, a noun of the verbal root), used for the thing grazed, in the way the verbal noun *al-khalq* (creation) is used to mean *al-makhluq* (the created thing), or it is an *ism makan al-ra'y* (a noun of place, the place of grazing), applied to what grows there and is grazed by way of a figurative usage (*majaz*), based on the relation of inherence (*'alaqat al-hulul*), just as the name *al-wadi* (the valley) is applied to the water flowing in it.

The indicator (*qarina*) is that He made it the object of *akhraja* (brought forth). The choice of the word *al-mar'a* over the word *al-nabat* (plants) is because the root *r-'-y* (grazing) suggests the benefit that livestock derive from it and the benefit that they provide to people who keep them, together with the requirement of the rhyme (*ri'ayat al-fasila*).

*Al-ghuthaa'* (debris, dry stubble): with a *damma* on the *ghayn*, and the *tha'* lightened; it is also said with the *tha'* doubled. It means the dry part of the plant.

*Al-ahwa'* is the one described as *al-hawwa*, with a *damma* on the *ha'* and a doubled *waw*. *Hawwa* is among the colors: a darkness that approaches black. It is an attribute of *ghuthaa'*, because the *ghuthaa'* is dry, so its greenness becomes *hawwa*.

This description, *ahwa'*, evokes the change of its color after it had been green and fresh. That is evidence of His exalted control over bringing into being and bringing to an end.

In the description of God's bringing forth the pasture and making it *ghuthaa'* *ahwa'*, together with the attributes that precede it, within the context of their relevance to the purpose for which the discourse was delivered, there is an allusion to portraying the state of the Qur'an, its guidance, and the law it contains that benefits people, by the state of the rain through which the pasture grows, so that beasts and livestock benefit from it. It also alludes to the fact that this law reaches completion and attains what God intended for it, just as the pasture reaches completion and attains its ripeness when it becomes dry *ahwa'*. This is in the manner of an implicit allegory (*tamthil makniyya*), signaled by mention of what necessarily accompanies the rain, which is the pasture. The explanation and detailing of this allusion has come in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The likeness of the guidance with which God has sent me is like abundant rain that fell upon a land. Part of it was fertile ground that absorbed the water and produced grass and abundant herbage. Part of it was barren ground that held the water, so God benefited people by it: they drank, gave drink, and cultivated." (The hadith continues.)

[Page 279]

It is also possible that the purpose of the clause ﴿so He made it dry debris, ahwa'﴾ is *idmaj al-'ibra* (embedding a lesson), by the variations of what God has placed in creatures of various stages from one thing to its opposite, to remind of extinction after life, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God is He who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair. He creates what He wills, and He is the Knowing, the Competent.﴾ [al-Rum: 54]. This indicates that the period of the freshness of life for things resembles a short period. Thus the particle that is placed for coordinating what the predicate applies to with what the predicate was applied to (*harf al-'atf*) is used for the coordination of *ja'alahu ghuthaa'an* (He made it debris). This is of the same kind as His words, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is like water We send down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingle with it, of what people and livestock eat,﴾ [Yunus: 24] down to His words: ﴿then We make it into stubble, as though it had not flourished yesterday.﴾ [Yunus: 24]

Since these are speeches, they relate to the name of God by virtue of its indication of the Essence. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 87, verses 6–7:

﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget, except what Allah wills. Indeed, He knows what is declared and what is hidden.﴾

You have already known that the command to glorify (tasbih, "glorify") in His words, ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [Al-A'la: 1], is a general good tidings to the Prophet ﷺ of a benefit that will come to him. Hence this is the place of clear explanation (bayan) with His promise that He will protect him from forgetting what He makes him recite, so that he conveys it as it was revealed to him and preserves it from slipping away from him. For this reason, this sentence is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), because good tidings create in the soul of the Prophet ﷺ an expectation of good that is coming to him. So He gave him the good news that He would increase him in revelation, along with what branches from His words, "We shall make you recite," from His words, "so you will not forget."

Since this surah is among the earliest surahs in order of revelation, and it is established in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Prophet ﷺ used to experience hardship in receiving the revelation when Jibril came down, and he would move his lips and tongue, wishing to memorize it and fearing that it would slip away from him. Forgetting (nisyan) is the absence of the previously known item from the memory of a person, for a moment or for a long time.

﷿ ﴿ونُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرى﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلا تَنْسى﴾ [al-A'la: 6]. The sentence ﴿إنَّهُ يَعْلَمُ الجَهْرَ وما يَخْفى﴾ [al-A'la: 7] is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ), as you have learned. This coordination is of the more general upon the more specific in its outcome, although the meaning of the preceding sentence differs from the meaning of facilitation (taysīr), because its meaning is preservation and protection, while the meaning of the coordinated clause is the facilitation of good for him.

Taysīr (facilitation) is making an action easy for its doer.

The object (maf'ūl) of the verb of facilitation is the thing that is made easy, i.e., not difficult. Along with the object, one mentions the thing for whose sake the act is made easy, marked with the preposition lām, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿ويَسِّرْ لِي أمْرِي﴾ [Ṭāhā: 26].

Page 282

al-Yusrā is the feminine of al-Aysar (the easiest/most favorable), and the pattern fuʿlā indicates intensity of the attribute, since it is the feminine of afʿal.

The modified noun is omitted, and the feminine form of the attribute indicates that the omitted noun is one that in speech is treated as feminine, either by being singular with a feminine marker or by being a plural, since plurals are treated as feminine. So the feminine attribute is understood as qualifying an implied noun suitable to the feminine in its form, and the context of the preceding speech points to the implied noun being the meaning of the sharīʿa (divine law), since the address of the Messenger ﷺ in the Qur'an takes into account his titular attribute, that he is a messenger. Therefore, the first of his affairs is surely what he was sent with, which is the sharīʿa.

His saying ﴿ونُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرى﴾: if it is taken according to the apparent structure of the speech, which is what the exegetes followed, then taysīr is used metaphorically for preparation and subjugation, i.e., the power of enabling him ﷺ to attain the easy matters and to act in them according to what God commands. That is, We prepare you for the easy affairs in matters of religion and their consequences: the facilitation of memorizing the Qur'an for you, the facilitation of the sharīʿa with which you were sent, and the facilitation of good for you in this world and the Hereafter. This metaphor is embellished by mushākala (correspondence in wording).

The meaning of the lām in His saying lil-yusrā is causation, i.e., for the sake of the easy matter, that is, for its acceptance. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Each is facilitated for that for which he was created." This verse follows the pattern of His saying: ﴿فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرى﴾ [al-Layl: 7] and His saying: ﴿فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرى﴾ [al-Layl: 10] in Surat al-Layl.

It is also possible that the speech is taken as deviating from the apparent requirement by using the figure of inversion (qalb), and that the original is: "We facilitate the easy matter for you," i.e., We make it easy for you so that it does not burden you. Then the verb nuyassiruka remains in its literal sense, and its action was changed in its object and the prepositional phrase attached to it, contrary to what is common in its object and the prepositional phrase attached to it.

Describing it as al-yusrā indicates the firmness of his facilitation of it, since it has been made easy, so nothing remains but his being protected from the obstacles with which receiving the easy matter would be difficult.

So the speech includes two facilitations: the facilitation of what the Prophet ﷺ was charged with, i.e., making it easy while still fulfilling its intended purpose, and the facilitation of the Prophet ﷺ for performing what he was charged with.

The deviation from the apparent requirement of the structure to what the structure has come upon may be justified: in it is the assignment of the facilitated thing to the place of the thing to which it is facilitated, and the reverse, for the sake of emphasis on the attribution of the act to the object, in the accepted manner of inversion, like the Arabs' saying: "The she-camel was presented to the water-trough," and the words of al-'Ajjaj:

"And a desert waste whose sides are dusty, as if the color of its earth were its sky."

Inversion occurs in verses of the Qur'an, among them His saying: ﴿ما إنَّ مَفاتِحَهُ لَتَنُوءُ بِالعُصْبَةِ أُولِي القُوَّةِ﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 76], and from it is the inverted simile (al-tashbīh al-maqlūb).

The meaning: God's promise to him that He facilitated for him the reception of the burdens of the message, so that it does not weigh upon him or distress him, as reassurance to him, since at the beginning of his mission he was anxious that he would not fulfil its obligations. That is, God made him capable of receiving perfections and the great matters of managing the community, which by their nature would weigh upon those who undertake their like.

Among the effects of this facilitation is what is reported in the hadith that the Messenger of God ﷺ "was never given a choice between two matters except that he chose the easier of them," and his saying ﷺ to his companions: "You were sent only as facilitators, not as makers of hardship."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 87, verse 9–13:

﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits.﴾ ﴿He who fears will be reminded.﴾ ﴿But the most wretched will avoid it.﴾ ﴿He who will burn in the greatest Fire.﴾ ﴿Then he will neither die therein nor live.﴾

After Allah had made His Messenger ﷺ firm, He undertook for him what removed his fear regarding the burdens of the Message, and what set his soul at rest concerning the repelling of what he feared of weakness in delivering the Message in its proper manner. He also undertook for him the prevention of forgetting what was revealed to him, except what Allah the Exalted willed to be forgotten. And His promise that He had granted him success, prepared him for that, and made it easy for him, since the Messenger ﷺ, at the beginning of his period with the Message (for this surah was the eighth of the surahs), did not know what Allah would entrust to him, and so he feared that he might fall short of the will of Allah, and that anger or blame from Him would befall him. Following this, He commanded him to remind, that is, to convey, that is, to persist in it, sharpening his resolve and stirring his energy, so that his devotion to reminding would be with his whole being. For when the obedience to a command is supported by the soul's eagerness to do what is commanded, there is delight for the one commanded; thus he combined the performance of the duty with the satisfaction of the heart.

So the fa' (فَ) is for consequence, following what preceded it, as the consequence of a result follows its premises.

The imperative (الأمر) is used to request continuity.

Reminding (التَّذْكِيرُ) is conveying the Reminder (الذِّكْر), which is the Qur'an.

Al-Dhikra (الذِّكْرى) is the verbal noun of reminding, and it has been discussed in Surat 'Abasa.

The object of fa-dhakkir (فَذَكِّرْ) is omitted for the sake of generality, that is, "so remind the people," and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾ — the two verses.

The clause ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the clause that is caused and its cause, and this parenthesis is considered with regard to the generality required by the omission of the object of fa-dhakkir. That is: "So persist in reminding all the people, if the reminder benefits all of them," that is, while it benefits only some, namely those who are understood from His saying: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾, and so on.

Thus the condition in His saying ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾ is a parenthetical clause, and it is not attached to the clause nor a restriction of its content, for the meaning is not: "So remind if the reminder has benefit," such that by way of the implication of contrast one would understand that you should not remind when the reminder does not benefit, since there is no basis for restricting reminding to when the reminder is beneficial, as there is no way to know the places where the reminder benefits. For this reason His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an those who fear My threat﴾ [Qaf: 45] has been interpreted as meaning: "So remind by the Qur'an, and whoever fears My threat will be reminded." Rather, what is intended is: "So remind the people all together, if the Reminder benefits all of them." Thus the condition is used to express uncertainty, because the original function of the conditional particle in (إنْ) is that its occurrence is not certain. The call is general, and what Allah knows of the states of people regarding acceptance of guidance or its absence is a matter whose knowledge Allah has kept to Himself. Abu Jahl was called to faith, and Allah knew that he would not believe, but Allah did not restrict the call to those from whom faith is hoped, to the exclusion of others, and reality reveals what is decreed.

This is an allusion that among the people there are those whom the Reminder does not benefit, and this is understood from the use of the particle in (إنْ), which requires the non-likelihood of the condition's occurrence or its rarity. For this reason it came after it with His saying:

﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾. This is an explanatory resumption (اسْتِئْنافٌ بَيانِيٌّ) arising from His saying "fa-dhakkir" and what was attached to it of the parenthesis by His saying ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾, indicating that the reminding does not benefit all those who are reminded.

This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "It benefits My friends and does not benefit My enemies." In this is what shows you the meaning of the verse clearly, free of any doubt, and it removes the perplexity of many of the exegetes regarding the interpretation of the meaning of in (إنْ). There is no need for the estimation of al-Farra' and al-Nahhas: "if the reminder benefits, and if it does not benefit," and that he confined himself to one division because it indicates the second.

Yadhdhakkaru (يَذَّكَّرُ) is the reflexive form of dhakkarahu. Its origin is yatadhakkaru, and the ta' was changed to dhal because their points of articulation are close, so that its assimilation into the other dhal could occur.

And ﴿man yakhshā﴾ (مَن يَخْشى) denotes a genus, not a specific individual; that is, "those who fear will be reminded." The hidden pronoun in yakhsha is treated in agreement with the word "man," since it is a singular word.

The verb yakhsha has been treated as intransitive, so no object was estimated for it, that is: "he will remind himself, from fear, of his thought and his nature," that is, he who anticipates the occurrence of harm and benefit, so he looks into the places of each and reflects upon the evidences, because he fears that what he was warned of will be fulfilled upon him.

Al-khashya (الخَشْيَةُ) is fear. It was discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44] in Surat Ta-Ha. Khashya has degrees, and in its levels believers differ.

Al-tajannub (التَّجَنُّبُ) is distancing oneself. Its origin is the form tafa"ala, indicating the effort of being situated at the side of something.

Al-janib (الجانِبُ) is the place which is the edge of something else, and the effort of being situated in it is a metaphor for seeking distance, that is, in a place far from it. That is, he distances himself from the Reminder, the most wretched.

The definite article in al-ashqa (الأشْقى) is the definite article of the genus, that is, "the most wretched ones."

Al-ashqa is one who is extremely wretched. Shiqwa and shaqa' in the language of the Shari'a are the state arising in the Hereafter from disbelief, of the condition of humiliation and punishment. In our view, whoever is known to have died as a believer is not wretched.

So al-ashqa is the disbeliever, because he is the most wretched of people in the Hereafter, due to his abiding in the Fire.

The definite article in al-ashqa is the definite article of the genus, so it includes all polytheists. Some exegetes took it to refer to a specific known person, and said: it refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, or 'Utba ibn Rabi'a.

The description of al-ashqa by ﴿who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾ is because the application of "al-ashqa" in this verse was at the beginning of the period of the Muhammadan mission, so there was in it an ambiguity requiring clarification, and so it was followed by a description that clarifies it in general terms, from what was revealed of the Qur'an before this verse.

The contrast of ﴿he who fears﴾ with al-ashqa indicates that the most wretched is one who by nature does not fear; he is heedless in his delusion, immersed in his amusement, and so he does not seek for himself deliverance from his wretchedness.

The description of the Fire as "the greatest" (الكُبْرى) is for terror and warning, and what is meant by it is Jahannam.

The clause ﴿then he will neither die therein nor live﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿will burn in the greatest Fire﴾, so it is a second relative clause.

Thumma (ثُمَّ) is for the graded sequence (التَّراخِي الرُّتْبِيِّ), indicating that what it conjoins is of greater rank in the purpose the speech is directed at, which is the intensity of punishment. For the perpetual state of being between life and death while in the torment of burning is a punishment more severe than what was conveyed by his being in the torment of burning. This is obvious, since burning is an event, and a degree has been added to it: that there is no rest from it by death, nor escape from it by life.

So the meaning of ﴿he will not die﴾ is: his perception does not cease, for death is the loss of perception, together with the wonder of this state, which is among what confirms the consideration of graded sequence in this severe punishment.

Its being followed by His saying ﴿nor live﴾ is a precaution to prevent the supposition that by negating death from them is meant that they have rested from the punishment, according to what is commonly known: that burning destroys the one burned. So if it were said "he will not die," those warned would suppose that this burning does not reach the level of destruction, and the burned one remains alive, and so it would be thought to be a mild burning, and would be a consolation to those threatened. To prevent this, He followed it with ﴿nor live﴾, that is, a life free of pains. The indication of the stated description is the contrast of "nor live" with His saying ﴿will burn in the greatest Fire﴾ and ﴿then he will not die therein﴾.

This is not of the kind of negating two attributes to establish an intermediate state between their two states, like ﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [An-Nur: 35] and the saying of one of the women of Umm Zar': "neither heat nor cold." For that has no purpose beneath it.

It is permissible that we make the negation of life a metaphor for the negation of deliverance, on the basis that the necessary consequence of burning is destruction, and the necessary consequence of life is non-destruction.

In the verse there is the embellishment of tibaq (antithesis), for the apparent opposition between "lā yamūtu" and "lā yaḥyā."

So the fa' (فَ) is for consequence, following what preceded it, as the consequence of a result follows its premises.

Al-Dhikra (الذِّكْرى) is the verbal noun of reminding, and it has been discussed in Surat 'Abasa.

The object of fa-dhakkir (فَذَكِّرْ) is omitted for the sake of generality, that is, "so remind the people," and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾ — the two verses.

The clause ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the clause that is caused and its cause, and this parenthesis is considered with regard to the generality required by the omission of the object of fa-dhakkir. That is: "So persist in reminding all the people, if the reminder benefits all of them," that is, while it benefits only some, namely those who are understood from His saying: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾, and so on.

Thus the condition in His saying ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾ is a parenthetical clause, and it is not attached to the clause nor a restriction of its content, for the meaning is not: "So remind if the reminder has benefit," such that by way of the implication of contrast one would understand that you should not remind when the reminder does not benefit, since there is no basis for restricting reminding to when the reminder is beneficial, as there is no way to know the places where the reminder benefits. For this reason His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an those who fear My threat﴾ [Qaf: 45] has been interpreted as meaning: "So remind by the Qur'an, and whoever fears My threat will be reminded." Rather, what is intended is: "So remind the people all together, if the Reminder benefits all of them." Thus the condition is used to express uncertainty, because the original function of the conditional particle in (إنْ) is that its occurrence is not certain. The call is general, and what Allah knows of the states of people regarding acceptance of guidance or its absence is a matter whose knowledge Allah has kept to Himself. Abu Jahl was called to faith, and Allah knew that he would not believe, but Allah did not restrict the call to those from whom faith is hoped, to the exclusion of others, and reality reveals what is decreed.

This is an allusion that among the people there are those whom the Reminder does not benefit, and this is understood from the use of the particle in (إنْ), which requires the non-likelihood of the condition's occurrence or its rarity. For this reason it came after it with His saying:

﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾. This is an explanatory resumption (اسْتِئْنافٌ بَيانِيٌّ) arising from His saying "fa-dhakkir" and what was attached to it of the parenthesis by His saying ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾, indicating that the reminding does not benefit all those who are reminded.

This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "It benefits My friends and does not benefit My enemies." In this is what shows you the meaning of the verse clearly, free of any doubt, and it removes the perplexity of many of the exegetes regarding the interpretation of the meaning of in (إنْ). There is no need for the estimation of al-Farra' and al-Nahhas: "if the reminder benefits, and if it does not benefit," and that he confined himself to one division because it indicates the second.

Yadhdhakkaru (يَذَّكَّرُ) is the reflexive form of dhakkarahu. Its origin is yatadhakkaru, and the ta' was changed to dhal because their points of articulation are close, so that its assimilation into the other dhal could occur.

And ﴿man yakhshā﴾ (مَن يَخْشى) denotes a genus, not a specific individual; that is, "those who fear will be reminded." The hidden pronoun in yakhsha is treated in agreement with the word "man," since it is a singular word.

The verb yakhsha has been treated as intransitive, so no object was estimated for it, that is: "he will remind himself, from fear, of his thought and his nature," that is, he who anticipates the occurrence of harm and benefit, so he looks into the places of each and reflects upon the evidences, because he fears that what he was warned of will be fulfilled upon him.

Al-khashya (الخَشْيَةُ) is fear. It was discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44] in Surat Ta-Ha. Khashya has degrees, and in its levels believers differ.

Al-tajannub (التَّجَنُّبُ) is distancing oneself. Its origin is the form tafa"ala, indicating the effort of being situated at the side of something.

Al-janib (الجانِبُ) is the place which is the edge of something else, and the effort of being situated in it is a metaphor for seeking distance, that is, in a place far from it. That is, he distances himself from the Reminder, the most wretched.

The definite article in al-ashqa (الأشْقى) is the definite article of the genus, that is, "the most wretched ones."

Al-ashqa is one who is extremely wretched. Shiqwa and shaqa' in the language of the Shari'a are the state arising in the Hereafter from disbelief, of the condition of humiliation and punishment. In our view, whoever is known to have died as a believer is not wretched.

So al-ashqa is the disbeliever, because he is the most wretched of people in the Hereafter, due to his abiding in the Fire.

The definite article in al-ashqa is the definite article of the genus, so it includes all polytheists. Some exegetes took it to refer to a specific known person, and said: it refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, or 'Utba ibn Rabi'a.

The description of al-ashqa by ﴿who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾ is because the application of "al-ashqa" in this verse was at the beginning of the period of the Muhammadan mission, so there was in it an ambiguity requiring clarification, and so it was followed by a description that clarifies it in general terms, from what was revealed of the Qur'an before this verse.

The contrast of ﴿he who fears﴾ with al-ashqa indicates that the most wretched is one who by nature does not fear; he is heedless in his delusion, immersed in his amusement, and so he does not seek for himself deliverance from his wretchedness.

The description of the Fire as "the greatest" (الكُبْرى) is for terror and warning, and what is meant by it is Jahannam.

The clause ﴿then he will neither die therein nor live﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿will burn in the greatest Fire﴾, so it is a second relative clause.

Thumma (ثُمَّ) is for the graded sequence (التَّراخِي الرُّتْبِيِّ), indicating that what it conjoins is of greater rank in the purpose the speech is directed at, which is the intensity of punishment. For the perpetual state of being between life and death while in the torment of burning is a punishment more severe than what was conveyed by his being in the torment of burning. This is obvious, since burning is an event, and a degree has been added to it: that there is no rest from it by death, nor escape from it by life.

So the meaning of ﴿he will not die﴾ is: his perception does not cease, for death is the loss of perception, together with the wonder of this state, which is among what confirms the consideration of graded sequence in this severe punishment.

Its being followed by His saying ﴿nor live﴾ is a precaution to prevent the supposition that by negating death from them is meant that they have rested from the punishment, according to what is commonly known: that burning destroys the one burned. So if it were said "he will not die," those warned would suppose that this burning does not reach the level of destruction, and the burned one remains alive, and so it would be thought to be a mild burning, and would be a consolation to those threatened. To prevent this, He followed it with ﴿nor live﴾, that is, a life free of pains. The indication of the stated description is the contrast of "nor live" with His saying ﴿will burn in the greatest Fire﴾ and ﴿then he will not die therein﴾.

This is not of the kind of negating two attributes to establish an intermediate state between their two states, like ﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [An-Nur: 35] and the saying of one of the women of Umm Zar': "neither heat nor cold." For that has no purpose beneath it.

It is permissible that we make the negation of life a metaphor for the negation of deliverance, on the basis that the necessary consequence of burning is destruction, and the necessary consequence of life is non-destruction.

In the verse there is the embellishment of tibaq (antithesis), for the apparent opposition between "lā yamūtu" and "lā yaḥyā."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 87, verses 14–15:**

﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself,﴾ ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord and prays.﴾

This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf bayani*, a resumption that answers an implied question). The mention of ﴿those who fear﴾ [al-A'la: 10] and the mention of ﴿the most wretched﴾ arouse the listener's expectation to learn the outcome of each. So the discourse begins by describing the consequence of wretchedness, that ﴿he shall enter the greatest Fire﴾ [al-A'la: 12], and the reward of ﴿the most pious﴾ is postponed, because the more important purpose of the passage is to explain the requital of the most wretched, who turn away from the Reminder. The listener remains waiting to learn the reward of the one who fears and takes heed. When the admonition and warning have been fulfilled, the speech is resumed to explain the reward and to encourage.

Thus, what is meant by ﴿he who purifies himself﴾ here is the same as what is meant by ﴿he who fears﴾ [al-A'la: 10] and ﴿takes heed﴾ (*yadhdhakkaru*). Here he is known as the one who ﴿remembers the name of his Lord﴾. Therefore, remembering the name of one's Lord is undoubtedly the taking heed through the Reminder, and taking heed is the goal of the Reminder which the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to deliver in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So remind﴾.

All kinds of good are gathered in His saying ﴿He has indeed succeeded (*aflaha*)﴾. Success (*al-falah*) is a person's attainment of what he aspires to, so it combines the meanings of triumph and benefit, and that is the achieving of the sought-after good. It has been discussed earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the successful﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

The use of the past tense verb in ﴿aflaha﴾ serves to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence in the Hereafter. Its being combined with the particle *qad*, which confirms and reinforces it, is as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], and His saying: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. This is because the address is directed to the wretched who turned away from the Reminder, in order to stir their resolve to join those who feared and so succeeded.

The meaning of *tazakka* is: he strove to become pure (*zakiyyan*), that is, he exerted his ability to cleanse and purify his soul, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9] ﴿and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [al-Shams: 10].

[Page 288]

The root form *tafa''ala* (*tazakka*) indicates exertion and the expenditure of effort. The origin of this is monotheism and the readiness for the righteous deeds that Islam brought and continues to bring, so it includes the giving of zakat on wealth.

Al-Bazzar related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said regarding ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself﴾: "It is the one who testifies that there is no god but Allah, renounces the rivals (*al-andad*), and testifies that I am the Messenger of Allah." And regarding ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾: "It refers to the five prayers, and maintaining them and being attentive to them." This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Qatadah.

He placed *tazakki* before the remembrance of Allah and the prayer because it is the root of acting upon all of that. When the soul is purified, the lights of guidance shine within it, so it knows their benefits and turns to them more. Thus *tazakki* is the training of oneself to accept good, and what is meant is purification through faith.

The verb in ﴿remembers the name of his Lord﴾ may be from the oral remembrance (*dhikr lisani*), which is with a kasra on the *dhal*. In that case the phrase ﴿the name of his Lord﴾ means the mention of Allah's names with glorification, such as saying (*la ilaha illa Allah*), (*Allahu akbar*) and (*subhana Allah*), and the like, as has been discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1].

It may also be from remembrance (*dhukr*), with a damma on the *dhal*, which is the presence of a thing in the mind that remembers and reflects. In that case the word *ism* (name) is inserted to indicate the greatness of Allah and the attributes of His majesty, since the names of Allah are attributes of perfection.

The consequence (*tafri'*) of ﴿and prayed (*fasalla*)﴾ upon ﴿remembers the name of his Lord﴾ holds under both interpretations, because remembrance in both its senses prompts the one who remembers to glorify Allah, Exalted is He, and to draw near to Him through prayer, which is submission and praise.

These three qualities in the verse have been arranged in the order in which they arise from one another. Their foundation is the removal of spiritual corruption, from false beliefs and from the soul's preoccupation with corrupt inner intentions, and this is what is indicated by His saying ﴿purifies himself (*tazakka*)﴾. Then comes the recollection of knowledge of Allah through the attributes of His perfection and wisdom, so that he fears and hopes in Him, and this is indicated by His saying ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord﴾. Then comes turning to obedience and worship of Him, which is indicated by His saying ﴿and prayed﴾. Prayer points to worship, and it is in itself obedience and compliance, after which come the other prescribed deeds. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 87, verses 16–17:

Page 289
﴿Nay, you prefer the worldly life,﴾ ﴿while the Hereafter is better and more enduring.﴾.
The majority (al-Jumhur) read tu'thirun with a feminine (second-person) form of address, and the address is directed to the polytheists by the context, and this is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). Abu 'Amr alone read it with the ya' (third-person) form, in the manner of ghaybah (third person), referring back to "the most wretched" [al-A'la: 11] ﴿who will enter the greatest Fire﴾ [al-A'la: 12].

The comprehensive meaning of the particle bal is idrab (turning away, change of direction). That is, the speech or the judgment turns to what comes after bal. So when it coordinates single words, the idrab is a cancellation of the preceding term, either because of an error in mentioning the coordinated term or to guard against it, and that is a turning away from the judgment. When it coordinates sentences, its coordination is the coordination of one utterance upon another, a purely verbal coordination free of sharing in the judgment, and it occurs in two ways. Sometimes the intent is to cancel the meaning of the preceding utterance, like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Or do they say, "He has madness"? Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70], which is a turning away in judgment. And sometimes the intent is merely the transition from one report to another without cancelling the first, like the words of the Exalted: ﴿And with Us is a Book which speaks with truth, and they will not be wronged. Rather, their hearts are in confusion﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 62]. Here bal is in the position of their saying "leave this aside," and this is a verbal turning away. One of the two idrabs is recognized by the indicators and the context.

Here bal coordinates a sentence by a formal coordination. It may be for the mere transition from mentioning those who benefit from the reminder and those who avoid it, to mentioning the cause of the turning away of those who avoid it, namely the wretched, that the cause is their preferring the worldly life. This is clear according to the reading of Abu 'Amr. As for the reading of the majority, it is an idrab from relating the conditions of the two groups, by transition to rebuking one of the two groups, namely the wretched group. So the address is directed to them by way of iltifat, to renew the attentiveness of the listener, so that the whole surah does not pass in reporting about them in the third person.

It may also be that the idrab is a cancellation of what was implied by His words: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ [al-A'la: 14], from the allusion to those who were wretched, by urging them to seek success for themselves so that they might join those who fear and purify themselves, so that they would be cut off from being the likely attainers of success.

The meaning: they are far from being presumed to compete in seeking success, because they prefer the worldly life. So the meaning is: "Rather, you prefer the benefits of the world over the portions of the Hereafter." This is like the adviser who says to a person whom he thinks will not accept advice: "I have advised you, and I do not think you will act on it."

Page 290
Both of the preceding possibilities, of address and third person, also apply here according to the two readings.
Al-iytha' (preference) is choosing something from among several options.

The meaning: you prefer the worldly life with your care and concern.

The object preferred over is not mentioned, because "the worldly life" indicates it; that is, you do not reflect on anything beyond this life of yours, nor do you reflect on a second life. The polytheists do not believe in the Hereafter, and when they are reminded of the Hereafter life and informed of it, they do not give their hearing to it and regard it as vain speech, and this is the point of rebuke.

Know that the believers too have a share of this admonition throughout time, and that share is proportionate to the amount of what one of them neglects of that which saves him in the Hereafter, preferring the benefits of the world which draw upon him a consequence in the Hereafter, according to what the Shari'ah has brought. As for increasing the benefits of the world while not neglecting the means of salvation in the Hereafter, that is a field for ambitions, and it is not a matter of blame. The Exalted said: ﴿But seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of the world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77].

The clause ﴿and the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ is coordinated to the clause of rebuke, a coordination of a report upon an imperative, because this report adds to the rebuke direction and confirmation, that in their aversion from reflecting on the signs of a life to come, they have turned away from what is better and more enduring.

Abqa (more enduring): an elative form, meaning more lasting in duration. And in the hadith forbidding dragging the lower garment, "let it be down to the ankles, for that is more pious and more enduring."

**Qur'an 87:18–19:** ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls,﴾ ﴿the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.﴾
